parts.problem_md:
Which row identifies the functional groups and structural formula of 4-hydroxybutanenitrile?

|   | **group 1** | **group 2** | **structural formula** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | carboxyl | amide | HOOCCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub> |
| **B** | hydroxyl | amine | HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> |
| **C** | hydroxyl | nitrile | CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CN |
| **D** | hydroxyl | nitrile | HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The prefix hydroxy– indicates a hydroxyl group (–OH)
- The suffix –nitrile indicates a nitrile group (–C≡N)
- In a nitrile, the carbon of the –C≡N group is always C1 of the parent chain
- But– indicates a four-carbon chain including the nitrile carbon: C1(–C≡N)–C2–C3–C4
- 4-hydroxy places the –OH on C4, the far end of the chain, giving HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN

**A** is incorrect as it contains a carboxyl group (–COOH) and an amide group (–CONH<sub>2</sub>); neither matches the functional groups in 4-hydroxybutanenitrile.

**B** is incorrect as it contains an amine group (–NH<sub>2</sub>) rather than a nitrile group (–C≡N). The –nitrile suffix specifies –C≡N, not –NH<sub>2</sub>.

**C** is incorrect as it contains –OH and –C≡N but the structural formula CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CN places the hydroxyl group on C3, making it 3-hydroxybutanenitrile, not 4-hydroxybutanenitrile.

parts.problem_md:
What is the systematic name of the molecule shown?

![Displayed formula of a branched pentane chain with a chloro group and a methyl group as substituents](assets/002-displayed-formula-of-a-branched-pentane-chain-wi.jpg)
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Identify the longest carbon chain: five carbons, so the parent chain is pentane

![Displayed formula of the molecule with the longest five-carbon chain highlighted](assets/003-displayed-formula-of-the-molecule-with-the-longe.jpg)

- Number the chain from the end that gives the lowest values:

  - The chloro group at C2
  - The methyl group at C3 (combination 2,3) is lower than 3,4
- The –CH<sub>3</sub> group is named methyl; the –Cl is named chloro
- Substituents are listed alphabetically: chloro before methyl
- Systematic name: 2-chloro-3-methylpentane

**A** is incorrect as the longest chain is five carbons (pentane), not four (butane). The –CH<sub>3</sub> branch is part of the longest chain, not an ethyl substituent.

**C** is incorrect as the longest chain is five carbons (pentane), not four (butane). The substituents are also listed in the wrong order.

**D** is incorrect as numbering from the wrong end of the chain gives positions 3 and 4, not the lowest possible 2 and 3.

parts.problem_md:
What is the systematic name of the molecule shown?

![Structural formula showing CH3-CH2-C(CH3)=C(CH3)-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH3](assets/004-structural-formula-showing-ch3-ch2-c-ch3-c-ch3-c.png)
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The longest carbon chain has seven carbons so the stem of the name is hept-
- The double bond is in position 3 because this is the lowest possible number
- The methyl groups are in positions 3, 4 and 5

![ocr-as-4-1h-mcq-q1-longest-chain](assets/005-ocr-as-4-1h-mcq-q1-longest-chain.png)

**B** is incorrect as the double bond must be in the position with the lowest possible number

**C** is incorrect as the longest possible chain is seven carbons not five

**D** is incorrect as the longest possible chain is seven carbons not six

parts.problem_md:
Xylitol is an artificial sweetener used in toothpaste.

![Structural formula of xylitol showing a five-carbon chain with five hydroxyl groups, two at the terminal carbons (primary alcohols) and three on the internal carbons (secondary alcohols)](assets/006-structural-formula-of-xylitol-showing-a-five-car.png)

Which functional groups are formed when xylitol is oxidised?

|   | **alkene** | **aldehyde** | **carboxylic acid** | **ketone** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | ⨯ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **B** | ⨯ | ✓ | ⨯ | ✓ |
| **C** | ⨯ | ✓ | ⨯ | ⨯ |
| **D** | ✓ | ⨯ | ⨯ | ⨯ |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Xylitol contains two primary alcohol groups at the ends of the carbon chain and three secondary alcohol groups on the internal carbons
- Primary alcohols oxidise to aldehydes (under limited oxidation) and to carboxylic acids (under complete oxidation with excess oxidising agent)
- Secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones
- All three of these functional groups (aldehyde, carboxylic acid, ketone) could therefore be produced

**B** is incorrect as it excludes carboxylic acid. Primary alcohols can be fully oxidised to carboxylic acids under suitable conditions.

**C** is incorrect as it excludes both carboxylic acid and ketone. Secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones.

**D** is incorrect as an alkene cannot be produced by oxidation of an alcohol. Alkene formation requires an elimination (dehydration) reaction, not oxidation.

parts.problem_md:
Which row correctly identifies the hydrocarbon molecules?

![Four molecules labelled 1 to 4: molecules 1 and 2 contain only carbon and hydrogen; molecules 3 and 4 contain additional elements](assets/007-four-molecules-labelled-1-to-4-molecules-1-and-2.jpg)

|   | **1** | **2** | **3** | **4** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | **✓** | **✓** | **✓** | **✓** |
| **B** | **✓** | **✓** | **✓** | **⨯** |
| **C** | **✓** | **✓** | **⨯** | **⨯** |
| **D** | **⨯** | **⨯** | **⨯** | **✓** |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- A hydrocarbon is a compound containing carbon and hydrogen only
- Molecule 1 is represented by a skeletal formula; no heteroatoms are shown, so it contains only carbon and hydrogen
- Molecule 2 shows a displayed formula with only C–C and C–H bonds, confirming it is also a hydrocarbon
- Molecules 3 and 4 both contain elements other than carbon and hydrogen, so they are not hydrocarbons

**A** and **B** are incorrect as they include a tick for molecule 3, which contains a heteroatom and is not a hydrocarbon.

**D** is incorrect as it marks molecule 4 as the only hydrocarbon. Molecule 4 contains a heteroatom. Molecules 1 and 2 are the hydrocarbons.

parts.problem_md: Which molecule contains an aldehyde functional group?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- An aldehyde contains a carbonyl carbon (–C=O) bonded to at least one hydrogen atom
- In condensed structural formulas this is written as –CHO or CHO– (at the start of a chain)
- Molecule D contains a CHO– group at C1, confirming it is an aldehyde (specifically 3-hydroxypentanal)

![Displayed structural formula of an aldehyde group showing the carbonyl carbon bonded to one hydrogen and one carbon chain](assets/008-displayed-structural-formula-of-an-aldehyde-grou.png)

**A** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> contains a –CO– group flanked by two carbon chains, making it a ketone (pentan-2-one).

**B** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH contains a –COOH group. The similar notation –CHO (aldehyde) and –COOH (carboxylic acid) is a common source of confusion. In a carboxylic acid the carbonyl carbon is bonded to a hydroxyl group, not a hydrogen atom.

**C** is incorrect as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub> contains a –COO– linkage, which represents an ester (methyl propanoate).

parts.problem_md:
What is the systematic name of the molecule shown?

![Skeletal formula of a branched hexane chain with three methyl substituents at positions 2, 4 and 4](assets/009-skeletal-formula-of-a-branched-hexane-chain-with.png)
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Identify the longest carbon chain: six carbons, so the parent chain is hexane
- There are three –CH<sub>3</sub> methyl substituents: prefix trimethyl

![Skeletal formula with the longest six-carbon chain highlighted and methyl groups at C2, C4 and C4 labelled](assets/010-skeletal-formula-with-the-longest-six-carbon-cha.png)

- Number from the end that gives the lowest values:

  - Methyl groups at C2, C4, and C4 (combination 2,4,4) is lower than 3,3,5
- Systematic name: 2,4,4-trimethylhexane

**A** is incorrect as 2,3,3-tetramethylpentane is a different isomer; it has four methyl groups on a five-carbon chain.

**C** is incorrect as the longest continuous carbon chain contains six carbons (hexane), not five. A common mistake is to mistake the end of the chain for an ethyl branch on a pentane, giving the false name 2-ethyl-2,4-dimethylpentane.

**D** is incorrect as numbering from the wrong end of the chain places the methyl groups at C3, C3, and C5 instead of the lower C2, C4, C4.

parts.problem_md:
What is the name of the circled functional group?

![Structural formula of an organic molecule with a C=O carbonyl group bonded to two carbon atoms, with the carbonyl group circled](assets/011-structural-formula-of-an-organic-molecule-with-a.jpg)
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The circled group contains a C=O bond bonded to two other carbon atoms, making it a ketone
- In the molecule shown, one carbon is a –CH<sub>3</sub> group and the other is a –CH<sub>2</sub>– group

**A** is incorrect as an aldehyde also contains a C=O, but the carbonyl carbon is bonded to at least one hydrogen atom (–CHO), not two carbon atoms.

**B** is incorrect as an alkene contains a C=C double bond, not a C=O bond.

**C** is incorrect as a carboxylic acid contains a –COOH group, where the carbonyl carbon is bonded to a hydroxyl group (–OH).

parts.problem_md:
What is the correct formula for 1-fluoro-3-methylbut-2-ene?

| **A** | Displayed | ![Displayed formula of 1-fluoro-3-methylbut-2-ene with the methyl group incorrectly placed on carbon 2](assets/012-displayed-formula-of-1-fluoro-3-methylbut-2-ene-.jpg) |
|---|---|---|
| **B** | Empirical | C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>9</sub>F |
| **C** | Skeletal | ![Incorrect skeletal formula omitting the fluorine atom and double bond with the branch on the wrong carbon](assets/013-incorrect-skeletal-formula-omitting-the-fluorine.jpg) |
| **D** | Structural | CH<sub>2</sub>FCH<sub>2</sub>C(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub> |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The name 1-fluoro-3-methylbut-2-ene identifies the parent chain, double bond, and substituents:

  - Parent chain: but-2-ene — a four-carbon chain with a C=C double bond at C2
  - 1-fluoro: fluorine atom on C1
  - 3-methyl: methyl group (–CH<sub>3</sub>) on C3
- The molecular formula is C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>9</sub>F
- The ratio 5:9:1 cannot be simplified further, so the empirical formula equals the molecular formula: C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>9</sub>F

![Structural formulas showing the molecular and empirical formula derivation for 1-fluoro-3-methylbut-2-ene](assets/014-structural-formulas-showing-the-molecular-and-em.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as the displayed formula shown places the methyl group on the wrong carbon.

**C** is incorrect as the skeletal formula shown omits the fluorine atom and the C=C double bond, and places the branch on the wrong carbon.

**D** is incorrect as CH<sub>2</sub>FCH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> has no C=C double bond. It is the structural formula for 1-fluoro-3-methylbutane, the saturated compound.

parts.problem_md: What is the structural formula of 2,2-dibromo-4-methylhexane?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- For this type of question it's often easier to draw out the displayed structure of the molecule and then work out the correct structural formula
- Begin by drawing the carbon chain, hexane, in this case
- The side groups are:

  - Two bromine atoms (from 'dibromo') which must be on the second carbon
  - One methyl group, CH<sub>3</sub>, (from -4-methyl) on the fourth carbon

![Structural formula of a six‑carbon chain: CH₃–CBr₂–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₃, showing bonds to hydrogen and bromine atoms.](assets/015-structural-formula-of-a-six-carbon-chain-ch-cbr-.png)

- Transpose the displayed formula into a condensed structural formula

parts.problem_md:
Which row is correct?

|   | **Systematic name** | **General formula** | **Skeletal formula** | **Structural formula** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | 2-methylpropanal | C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>O | ![Skeletal formula of 2-methylpropanal](assets/016-skeletal-formula-of-2-methylpropanal.png) | CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CHO |
| **B** | 4-methylhexan-2-one | C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>O | ![Skeletal formula of 4-methylhexan-2-one](assets/017-skeletal-formula-of-4-methylhexan-2-one.png) | CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> |
| **C** | 4-methylpentylamine | C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+1</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> | ![Skeletal formula of 4-methylpentylamine](assets/018-skeletal-formula-of-4-methylpentylamine.png) | CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> |
| **D** | ethyl propanoate | C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>O<sub>2</sub> | ![Skeletal formula of ethylpropanoate](assets/019-skeletal-formula-of-ethylpropanoate.png) | CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The general formula for a ketone is C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>O
- The skeletal formula and CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> are correct for 4-methylhexan-2-one

**A** is incorrect as C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>O is the general formula for an alcohol, not an aldehyde. The general formula for an aldehyde is C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>O

**C** is incorrect as the systematic name is 2-methylpentylamine because the lowest possible number is used

**D** is incorrect as the structural formula should be CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. The ester linkage has been written in the wrong order

parts.problem_md:
Compound A, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, is produced by the oxidation of compound B, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O.

Which functional group is present in compound B?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Compound B (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O) fits the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>O, which corresponds to an alcohol

  - Alcohols contain a hydroxyl (–OH) functional group
- Compound A (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) is produced by oxidation of compound B, confirming B is a primary alcohol

C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>2</sub>

C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>13</sub>OH → C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>11</sub>COOH

![Reaction scheme showing the oxidation of hexan-1-ol (a primary alcohol) to hexanoic acid (a carboxylic acid)](assets/020-reaction-scheme-showing-the-oxidation-of-hexan-1.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as the carbonyl group (C=O) is present in compound A, not B.

**B** is incorrect as the carboxyl group (–COOH) is present in compound A, not B.

**C** is incorrect as an ester (general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) also matches compound A, but esters are formed by condensation reactions, not by simple oxidation of an alcohol.

parts.problem_md:
Limonene is found in the peel of citrus fruits.

![Skeletal formula of limonene](assets/021-skeletal-formula-of-limonene.png)

Which row gives the empirical and molecular formulae of limonene?

|   | Empirical formula | Molecular formula |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub> | C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>16</sub> |
| **B** | C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>9</sub> | C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>18</sub> |
| **C** | C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>13</sub> | C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>13</sub> |
| **D** | C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>16</sub> | C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>16</sub> |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Empirical formula is the simplest whole number ratio of atoms in a chemical formula
- Molecular formula is the actual number and type of atoms in a formula
- Counting up the number of C and H atoms in limonene and taking into account the two double bonds, gives a molecular formula of C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>16</sub> and an empirical formula of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub>

**B** is incorrect as the double bonds have been ignored, resulting in two extra hydrogens in the molecular formula, which also gives an incorrect empirical formula

**C** is incorrect as the CH<sub>3</sub> group has been missed, resulting in an incorrect molecular and empirical formula

**D** is incorrect as the molecular formula is correct, but it has not been simplified to give the empirical formula

> **[exam-tip]**
> To get the correct molecular formula, it can help to draw the molecule out with all atoms showing:
> 
> ![Blue skeletal formula of a benzene-like carbon ring with attached CH₃ and CH₂ groups, showing single and double bonds on a white background](assets/022-blue-skeletal-formula-of-a-benzene-like-carbon-r.png)
> 
> That way you are less likely to miss any atoms, especially hydrogens
